notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0060.tlg001.perseus-: The phrase σπέρμα συγγενὲς … ἡμέρας, ‘a seed akin to Day’, is obscure and the rendering is uncertain.
κυνῆ, here ‘dog-skin’, usually means a cap or helmet (originally one of dog's hide).
ἀπὸ τοῦ συμβεβηκότος ἱεροῦ πεδίου is compressed; it may instead mean the island is named from the holy field there. χοάς, ‘libations’, here seems to mean vessels for libations.

The Greek has Zathraustes for Zoroaster. The Arianoi are the people of Ariana in the Iranian east, not Christian Arians. τοῖς ἀπαθανατίζουσι, 'who make [men] immortal', may mean 'who believe themselves immortal'.
The Greek calls the city Ninos, after the king; rendered Nineveh.

nodes.text: Now the men of Egypt, when they came into being long ago, looking up at the cosmos and struck with amazement and wonder at the nature of the universe, supposed that there were two gods, eternal and first, the sun and the moon, of whom they named the one Osiris and the other Isis, each of these names having been given from a certain etymology.

The spirit, then, they named Zeus, as the word is translated; they held it, as the cause of the soul's life in living creatures, to be as it were a kind of father of all. And they say that the most illustrious of the poets among the Greeks also agrees with them, when he says of this god ‘father of men and gods’.
And fire, translated, they named Hephaestus, holding it to be a great god that contributes much to all things for their generation and full growth.

For the Egyptians consider Oceanus to be the river in their country, the Nile, beside which the births of the gods also took place; for of the whole inhabited world, Egypt alone has many cities founded by the ancient gods, such as [those] of Zeus, the Sun, Hermes, Apollo, Pan, Eileithyia, and many others.

Some of the priests say that Hephaestus was the first to reign, having become the discoverer of fire and having obtained the rule because of this service; for when a tree in the mountains was struck by lightning and the forest near it was burning, Hephaestus came up, and since it was the winter season he took exceptional pleasure in the warmth, and as the fire died down he kept throwing wood on it, and keeping the fire going in this way he invited the other men to the benefit that came from it.

After this Cronus ruled, and having married his sister Rhea he begot, according to some of the mythographers, Osiris and Isis, but according to most, Zeus and Hera, who because of their virtue became kings over the whole universe. From these were born five gods, one born on each of the five intercalary days among the Egyptians; and the names of the children were Osiris and Isis, and also Typhon and Apollo and Aphrodite;

For first, [they say,] they made the human race cease from eating one another, after Isis had discovered the fruit of wheat and barley, which grew at random throughout the land along with the other plants but was unknown to men, and Osiris had devised the preparation of these crops as well; and all gladly changed their food, both because of the pleasantness of the things discovered and because it seemed advantageous to abstain from their savagery against one another.

And they say that Osiris and his companions founded in the Thebaid in Egypt a city of a hundred gates, which they named after their mother, but which later generations call Diospolis, and some Thebes.

And [they say] that Osiris was also fond of farming, and that he was reared in Nysa, in Arabia Felix near Egypt, being a son of Zeus, and that he has his name among the Greeks from both his father and the place, being called Dionysus.

Osiris, then, they say, having settled the affairs of Egypt and handed over the government of the whole to his wife Isis, placed beside her Hermes as counsellor, because he surpassed his other friends in wisdom; and as general of all the land under his rule he left Heracles, who was his kinsman and admired for his courage and bodily strength; and as governors he appointed Busiris over the parts lying towards Phoenicia and the places by the sea, and Antaeus over those in the direction of Ethiopia and Libya; and he himself set out from Egypt with his army on the campaign, taking with him also his brother, whom the Greeks call Apollo.

Osiris, they say, was accompanied on the campaign by two sons, Anubis and Macedon, who were outstanding in courage. Both of them bore the most conspicuous arms, taken from certain animals not unsuited to their own daring; for Anubis put on a dog-skin cap, and Macedon the forepart of a wolf; and for this reason these animals are honoured among the Egyptians.

They also took Pan along on the campaign, who is especially honoured by the Egyptians; for the natives have made not only statues of him in every temple, but also a city named after him in the Thebaid, called by the natives Chemmo, which translated is City of Pan. There also followed men experienced in agriculture: Maron in the planting of the vine, and Triptolemus in the sowing of grain and the whole harvest.

For they say that Osiris, while reigning lawfully over Egypt, was killed by his brother Typhon, a violent and impious man; and that he divided the body of the murdered man into twenty-six pieces and gave a portion to each of those who had joined in the attack, wishing all to share in the pollution, and thinking that by this means he would have them as fellow-fighters and steadfast guardians of his kingship.
But Isis, being the sister and wife of Osiris, avenged the murder with the help of her son Horus, and having slain Typhon and his accomplices she reigned over Egypt.

Isis, then, [they say,] found all the parts of the body except the genitals; and wishing to keep her husband's grave unknown and yet honoured by all who dwell in Egypt, she accomplished her purpose in some such way as this. Around each of the parts, they say, she moulded a figure of human shape, like Osiris in size, out of spices and wax;
and that the sacred bulls, both the one called Apis and the Mnevis, were consecrated to Osiris, and that all the Egyptians in common were taught to worship these as gods;
Likewise she too, when she had departed from among men, received immortal honours and was buried at Memphis, where her shrine is shown to this day, lying in the precinct of Hephaestus.

But some say that the bodies of these gods lie not in Memphis but on the borders of Ethiopia and Egypt, on the island in the Nile which lies by the place called Philae and has the name ‘Holy Field’ from what happened [there].

As evidence of this they point to what remains on this island: the tomb built for Osiris, honoured in common by the priests throughout Egypt, and the three hundred and sixty libation bowls set around it;

For this reason this island too may not be set foot on by those who pass by. And all who inhabit the Thebaid, which is the most ancient part of Egypt, consider it the greatest oath when anyone swears by Osiris who lies in Philae. Now the parts of Osiris that were found, they say, were deemed worthy of burial in the manner described; but the genital member, they say, was thrown into the river by Typhon, because none of his accomplices was willing to take it, yet by Isis it was deemed worthy, no less than the other [parts], of honours equal to a god's; for she made an image of it in the temples and taught [men] to honour it, and in the rites and sacrifices performed for this god she made it most highly honoured and the object of the greatest reverence.

Wherefore the Greeks too, having received from Egypt what concerns the orgiastic rites and the Dionysiac festivals, honour this member in the mysteries and in the initiations and sacrifices of this god, calling it phallus.

Those who say that the god was born at Thebes in Boeotia of Semele and Zeus are, they say, improvising. For Orpheus, having come to Egypt and taken part in the initiation and shared in the Dionysiac mysteries, being a friend of the Cadmeans and honoured by them, transferred the god's birth [to Thebes] to gratify them; and the common people, partly through ignorance and partly through wishing the god to be thought a Greek, readily accepted the initiations and the mysteries.

that Cadmus, who came from the Egyptian Thebes, fathered among other children Semele; that she, seduced by someone or other, became pregnant and, when seven months had passed, bore an infant whose appearance was just such as the people of Egypt believe Osiris had at his birth; and that such a child is not usually born alive, whether because the gods do not wish it or because nature does not allow it. And that Cadmus, perceiving what had happened,
In general there is much disagreement about these gods. For the same [goddess] some call Isis, others Demeter, others Thesmophorus, others Selene, others Hera, and others call her by all these names.

Osiris some have held to be Sarapis, others Dionysus, others Pluto, others Ammon, some Zeus, and many Pan; and some say that Sarapis is the one named Pluto among the Greeks. And the Egyptians say that Isis was the discoverer of many drugs for health and had great experience of the science of medicine;

For [they say] that she stands over the sick in their sleep and gives them aid against their diseases, and that those who obey her are healed beyond expectation; and that many who have been despaired of by physicians because of the difficulty of their illness are saved by her, and that numbers who have been wholly maimed in their sight or in some other part of the body, whenever they take refuge with this goddess, are restored to their former condition.

And [they say] that she also discovered the drug of immortality, by which she not only raised up her son Horus, when he had been plotted against by the Titans and found dead in the water, giving [him back] his soul,

but also made him partake of immortality. And he seems to have been the last of the gods to reign, after his father Osiris departed from among men. They say that Horus, translated, is Apollo, and that, having been taught both medicine and divination by his mother Isis, he benefits the human race through his oracles and his healings.

I am not unaware that some of the historians declare that the tombs of these gods are in Nysa in Arabia, from which Dionysus too is called Nysaeus. And [they say] that there is also a stele of each of the gods inscribed in sacred letters.

On that of Isis, they say, is inscribed: “I am Isis, the queen of every land, she who was taught by Hermes, and whatever laws I have laid down, no one can undo. I am the eldest daughter of Cronus, the youngest god; I am wife and sister of Osiris the king; I am she who first discovered grain for men; I am mother of Horus the king; I am she who rises in the star that is in the Dog;

For me the city of Bubastus was built. Farewell, farewell, Egypt that nurtured me.” And on that of Osiris it is said to be inscribed: “My father is Cronus, the youngest of all the gods, and I am Osiris the king, who campaigned over every land as far as the uninhabited places of the Indians and those that lie towards the north, as far as the sources of the river Ister, and again to the other parts as far as the Ocean. I am the eldest son of Cronus, and, a shoot from a fair and noble egg, I was born a seed akin to Day. There is no place in the inhabited world to which I have not come, distributing to all the things of which I was the discoverer.”

Some say too that Daedalus, having visited Egypt and admired the skill in the work, built for Minos, who was king of Crete, a labyrinth like the one in Egypt, in which, the myth goes, the so-called Minotaur lived.

For [they say] that from his company with the astrologers, with whom he lived constantly, the king had gained experience of such things, and that the story of his changes of form was told in myth among the Greeks from the custom handed down to the kings.

For it was customary for the rulers of Egypt to put about their heads the foreparts of lions and bulls and serpents, as signs of their rule; and sometimes trees, sometimes fire, and at times also to carry on their heads not a little fragrant incense, and by these at once to adorn themselves for comeliness and to strike others with astonishment and superstitious awe.

Some give a reason for the honour paid to this bull, saying that when Osiris died his soul passed into it, and for this reason it continues to this day, at each installation of the bull, always to pass over to its successors;

The sacred bulls, I mean Apis and Mnevis, are honoured like the gods, as Osiris instituted, both because of their use in agriculture and because the fame of those who discovered the crops has been handed down through the labours of these [beasts] to later generations for all time. Red oxen are permitted to be sacrificed because Typhon is thought to have been of that colour, he who plotted against Osiris and was punished by Isis for the murder of her husband.

And men too of the same colour as Typhon, they say, were sacrificed in ancient times by the kings at the tomb of Osiris; now few of the Egyptians are found to be red, but most of the foreigners are; and so among the Greeks too the myth of Busiris's killing of strangers gained currency, though Busiris was not the name of a king, but the tomb of Osiris has this name in the language of the natives.

And among several other peoples too this kind of device is recorded as having been used and as having brought many benefits to those who were persuaded by it: for among the Arianians they relate that Zoroaster claimed that the good *daimōn* [divine spirit] gave him his laws, among the people called the Getae, who make [men] immortal, Zalmoxis [said] the same of the common Hestia, and among the Jews Moses [claimed it of] the god called Iao; whether because they judged a conception that would benefit a multitude of people to be altogether marvellous and divine, or because they supposed that the crowd, looking to the superiority and power of those said to have found the laws, would be the more obedient.

[He] calls the river Oceanus because the Egyptians in their own language call the Nile Oceanus; [he calls] the city of the Heliopolitans the gates of the Sun; and he gives the name of meadow, the mythical dwelling of the departed, to the place beside the lake called Acherusia, near Memphis, around which there are very beautiful meadows of marsh, lotus and reed. And it is consistent [with this] that the dead are said to dwell in these places, because most of the Egyptians' burials, and the greatest, take place there, the corpses being ferried across both the river and the Acherusian lake, and the bodies laid in the tombs that lie there.

They say that near these places there are also a shrine of dark Hecate and gates of Cocytus and of Lethe, fastened with bronze bars. And that there are other gates as well, of Truth, and near these stands a headless statue of Justice.

Of Homer's visit they bring forward various signs, and above all the drugging of Telemachus by Helen at Menelaus's [house], and the forgetting of the evils that had befallen. For the drug nepenthes, which the poet says Helen received from Egyptian Thebes, from Polydamna the wife of Thon, he has evidently examined with accuracy; for even now, they say, the women in this city use the aforementioned power, and among the women of Diospolis alone, they say, a drug against anger and grief has been found from ancient times; and Thebes and Diospolis are the same.
And Aphrodite is called ‘golden’ by the natives from an ancient tradition, and there is a plain called ‘of golden Aphrodite’ near the [city] named Momemphis.

The king of the Arabs, then, he honoured with gifts and magnificent spoils and sent back with his own army to his own land, while he himself, gathering forces from everywhere and supplies of everything needed, founded beside the river Euphrates a well-walled city, laying out its shape as an oblong. Each of the longer sides of the city was a hundred and fifty stades, and each of the shorter ones ninety.

In Syria, then, there is a city, Ascalon, and not far from it a large, deep lake full of fish. Beside it is the precinct of a famous goddess whom the Syrians call Derceto; she has the face of a woman, but all the rest of her body is that of a fish, for some such reasons as these.

The most learned of the natives relate in myth that Aphrodite, having taken offence at the aforementioned goddess, cast into her a terrible passion for a certain youth, not ill-looking, among those who offered sacrifice; and that Derceto, having lain with the Syrian, bore a daughter, but being ashamed of her misdeeds, made the youth disappear and exposed the child in some desert and rocky places; and that she herself, from shame and grief, threw herself into the lake and was changed in the form of her body into a fish; for which reason the Syrians to this day abstain from this creature and honour fish as gods.

And around the place where the infant was exposed, a great flock of doves was nesting, and by them the child was nurtured in a marvellous and divine way; for some, enfolding the infant's body with their wings on every side, kept it warm, while others, whenever they saw that the cowherds and the other herdsmen were away, carried milk in their beaks from the nearby farmsteads and fed it by dripping it between its lips.

So they at once carried it to the farmstead and gave it to the overseer of the royal herds, Simmas by name; and he, being childless, reared the child as his daughter with every care, giving her the name Semiramis, which in the language of the Syrians is a name derived from doves, which since those times all the people of Syria have continued to honour as goddesses.

and its breadth, as Ctesias says, ten. So, since the city lay on a plain beside the Euphrates, the mound could be seen from many stades away like an acropolis; and they say it remains to this day, although Nineveh was razed by the Medes when they overthrew the kingdom of the Assyrians. Semiramis, who was by nature given to great enterprises and eager for glory to surpass her predecessor on the throne, set about founding a city in Babylonia; and having chosen architects and craftsmen from everywhere, and furthermore having prepared all the other resources, she gathered from the whole kingdom two million men for the completion of the works.

After this she built in the middle of the city a temple of Zeus, whom the Babylonians, as we have said, call Belus. Since the historians disagree about this, and the structure has fallen down through time, it is not possible to state the exact truth. But it is agreed that it was exceedingly high, and that the Chaldaeans made their observations of the stars in it, the risings and settings being accurately observed because of the height of the structure.

The whole building having been made with costly artistry of asphalt and brick, at the top of the ascent she set up three statues of hammered gold, of Zeus, Hera and Rhea. Of these, that of Zeus was standing and striding forward, and being forty feet high it weighed a thousand Babylonian talents; that of Rhea, seated on a golden chair, had the same weight as the former; and at her knees stood two lions, and near by huge serpents of silver, each weighing thirty talents.

Some, telling it as myth, say that she became a dove and, when many birds had flown down to the house, flew away with them; and that this is why the Assyrians honour the dove as a deity, making Semiramis immortal. She, then, having ruled all Asia except the Indians, died in the manner described, having lived sixty-two years and reigned forty-two.

The Chaldaeans, then, being among the most ancient of the Babylonians, hold in the divisions of the state a position much like that of the priests in Egypt; for being appointed to the service of the gods, they spend their whole life in philosophy, having the greatest reputation in astrology. They also devote themselves much to divination, making predictions about the future, and they try to provide the averting of evils and the fulfilment of good things, some by purifications, some by sacrifices, and some by certain other incantations.

To Perses was born a daughter, Hecate, who surpassed her father in daring and lawlessness; being fond of hunting, when she had no luck she would shoot down men with her arrows instead of beasts. Being devoted to the art of compounding deadly drugs, she discovered the so-called aconite, and tested the power of each [poison] by mixing it into the food given to strangers. Having gained great experience in these things, she first destroyed her father with poison and succeeded to the kingship; then, having founded a temple of Artemis and instituted the sacrifice to the goddess of strangers who put in by sea, she became notorious for her cruelty.

When Theseus and his companions were about to sail, Aegeus made an agreement with the helmsman and instructed him that if Theseus overcame the Minotaur they should sail home with white sails, but if he perished, with black, as they had been accustomed to do before. When they had sailed to Crete, Ariadne, the daughter of Minos, fell in love with Theseus, who was outstanding for his good looks, and Theseus, entering into talk with her and gaining her as his helper, both killed the Minotaur and, having learned from her the way out of the labyrinth, escaped safely.

Through his ingenuity Pasiphae lay with the bull and bore the Minotaur of the myth. They say that he was of double nature, having the upper parts of the body as far as the shoulders [those] of a bull, and the rest [those] of a man.

These are also said to have been sorcerers, and to bring on, whenever they wished, clouds and rain and hail, and likewise to draw down snow; and these things, they relate, they did just as the magi do. They also changed their own shapes, and were jealous in teaching their crafts.

As evidence of this, they say, there remains [the fact] that many of the women even now take incantations from this god and make amulets, on the ground that he was a sorcerer and practised what concerns the mystery rites; and these are very far removed from the ways of the Heracles who was born of Alcmene.
